1:
After these things means, Calvin says, not merely the last vision but the whole run of them, and he sets out the run. Abraham had passed an unsettled life in continued exile to his eightieth year, harassed with injuries and living in continual trepidation; famine had driven him into Egypt; twice his wife had been torn from his bosom; he had rescued his nephew at the peril of his own life; he had lived childless while all his hopes hung on having offspring; and having at last obtained a son, he had been compelled to disinherit him and drive him far from home. Isaac alone remained, and he was enjoying peace at home when God thundered suddenly out of heaven. Ellicott describes the same lull: for twenty-five years the patriarch had wandered and seen the promise perpetually deferred without his faith failing, and now, at peace with his neighbours, with pasture enough and Isaac approaching manhood, everything seemed to presage a calm and happy old age. Henry puts it as the lesson it is — perhaps he was beginning to think the storms had all blown over, and after all this encounter comes, sharper than any yet; many former trials will not secure us from further ones, for we have not yet put off the harness. Gill collects the guesses at Isaac's age, from five, which he rejects because a child could hardly have carried the wood, up to the Targum's thirty-six.

The word rendered tempt gives all of them trouble. Clarke would avoid it: though tempt, from tento, signifies no more than to prove or try, it is now generally used to imply a solicitation to evil, in which way God never tempts any man. He prefers what the versions do with it — the Greek has tried, or pierced through, and Symmachus renders it glorified, taking the root to mean glistering with light, whence a banner displayed, so that God put great honour on Abraham by giving him this opportunity of showing to all successive ages the efficacy of an unshaken faith. Henry reaches the same reading by another route, noting that some render it he did lift up Abraham, as a scholar who improves well is lifted up into a higher form; and he adds the distinction plainly, that God tempted him not to draw him to sin, as Satan tempts, but to discover his graces.

What made this one unbearable is where Calvin and Ellicott do their best work. Calvin insists the wound was not chiefly paternal. Set beside the conflict of conscience, the bereavement and the violence and even the father's being made executioner are mere shadows of conflicts; the great source of grief was that in the person of this son the whole salvation of the world seemed to be extinguished. His contest was not with his carnal passions but with his own piety, since God, as if engaging him in personal combat, required the death of the boy to whose person he had himself annexed the hope of eternal salvation. The command was, in a certain sense, the destruction of faith: God shook the faith the holy man had placed in his word by a counter assault of the word itself. Ellicott puts the first half of the trial in a form the others do not reach. Human sacrifice was abhorrent to the nature of Jehovah, so Abraham's plain duty was to test the command, and no subjective proof would have served — had he been moved only by an internal impulse, his conduct would have deserved the same condemnation as the later Israelites who gave their firstborn in religious frenzy and got a deeper guilt for it. Only when he was satisfied that the command came from outside himself, and from the God he had so often conversed with, did the antecedents of his own life require obedience.
2:
Ellicott begins with the first word, which is not an adverb of time at all but an interjection of entreaty, ordinarily attached to requests to soften them, so that the sentence reads more as exhortation than command. What follows is a ladder, and Wesley climbs it rung by rung: not thy bullocks and thy lambs, which Abraham would willingly have parted with by thousands to redeem Isaac; not thy servant, no, not the steward of thine house; thy only son by Sarah, Ishmael being lately cast out, so that Isaac only was left — and must he go too? Yes: take Isaac, him by name, thy laughter, that son indeed. Clarke reports the same effect from Warburton, that the order of the words gradually increases the sense and raises the passions higher and higher, and adds Jarchi's suggestion that the minuteness was meant to preclude any doubt about who was intended. Ellicott sharpens the cruelty by comparison: if childlessness had been unendurable to Abraham before, what must it be now, after so many years' enjoyment of a son and after giving up Ishmael for his sake?

Where the land of Moriah was is disputed. Clarke takes it for the mountains of Jerusalem, Gihon or Calvary and Sion and Acra together, and passes on the conjecture that Abraham offered on the very mount where our Lord was afterwards crucified; he notes that Beersheba lies some forty-two miles off, so it is no wonder the party did not arrive until the third day. Ellicott weighs the rival claim of Moreh in Sichem, which many able commentators have urged and the Samaritans affirmed, placing the altar on the summit of Gerizim — and rejects it on three grounds: Gerizim is far too remote from Beersheba to be reached early on the third day, since even the journey to Jerusalem takes twenty and a half hours and travellers then had to cook their own food and make their own beds; Moriah is described as a land, some part of which Abraham was to be shown; and Moreh was a place he had lived in and knew already. On the name itself he allows two derivations, Jah is teacher or Jah is provider, and prefers the second, since it would then be drawn from this very event.

Whether a real killing was meant, Ellicott settles against Hengstenberg and others, who argued that Abraham was to surrender Isaac spiritually and sanctify him by a burnt offering rather than slay him — a reading contradicted both by the narrative itself and by the epistle, which locates the victory of Abraham's faith precisely in believing that though Isaac were killed the promise would still be fulfilled in him. Keil says the same from the other side, that the command was framed so that Abraham could understand it in no other way than as an outward burnt offering, since there was no other way to accomplish the complete surrender than by actually preparing to make the sacrifice; and he quotes Luther on the impasse, that human reason would simply conclude either that the promise is a lie or that the command comes from the devil and not from God, since if Isaac must be killed the promise is void, and if the promise stands this cannot be God's command. Calvin works the same knot and unties it the same way. Abraham was commanded to cut in pieces the very charter of his salvation, and his mind must have been severely crushed when the command and the promise of God were conflicting within him; but having concluded that the God he had to do with could not be his adversary, he reconciled the two by hope without seeing how, and left the unknown issue to Providence — going, meanwhile, as with closed eyes, whither he was directed.
3:
Henry lists what Abraham had to break through, and the list is not gentle. The command seemed directly against an antecedent law of God forbidding murder — can the unchangeable God contradict himself, and can he who hates robbery for burnt offering delight in murder for it? It could not be squared with natural affection: cannot Abraham be obedient without being unnatural, and must the father of the faithful be the monster of all fathers? No reason was given, where a reason had been given when Ishmael was cast out; and Isaac was neither a martyr nor a ransom nor a criminal but a dutiful, obedient, hopeful son, so that one may ask what profit there is in his blood. It could not be squared with the promise. And afterwards there was Sarah to face, with the blood of Isaac staining his raiment — surely a bloody husband hast thou been to me — and the Egyptians and Canaanites and Perizzites to hear of it, to the eternal reproach of Abraham and his altars. What answered every one of these, Henry says, was simply that he was infallibly assured the command was God's and no delusion; God's commands are not to be disputed but obeyed.

Calvin measures the obedience by the speed of it. Innumerable thoughts might have come into the holy man's mind, any one of which would have overwhelmed his spirit had he not fortified it by faith, and there is no doubt that Satan, during the darkness of that night, heaped upon him a vast mass of cares. To overcome them gradually by contending with them was heroical courage; but then immediately to gird himself to the command, and to rise early to do it, was a remarkable effort. Other men, prostrated by a message so dire, would have fainted and lain torpid as if deprived of life — and the first dawn was scarcely early enough for Abraham's haste. Henry and Wesley take the same rising as the first of the steps: he did not delay, did not demur, did not take time to deliberate, for those that do the will of God heartily will do it speedily, and while we delay time is lost and the heart hardened.

The preparations are given in detail, and Ellicott thinks that is the point of them — every step is minutely recorded, as if to show the calmness with which Abraham girded himself for obedience. He took the wood ready cleft, not because there was none to be had on the spot, but so that when they arrived there should be nothing to distract their thoughts and they might proceed at once to the sacrifice; Henry has him cleaving it with his own hands, and draws the general rule that spiritual sacrifices must be prepared for in the same way. Two of the silences Henry fills in. Sarah was very probably told nothing, lest she prevent it — there is so much in our own hearts to hinder our progress in duty that we have need to keep out of the way of other hindrances. And the servants were left at a distance lest they interpose and disturb so strange an oblation, as Christ, entering on his agony in the garden, took three disciples with him and left the rest behind. Clarke adds what the Targum supplies where the text is silent, that the two young men were Eliezer and Ishmael, and the wood small wood, fig and palm, proper for a burnt offering. Gill takes the command to have come in a dream or vision of the night, which is why the morning is the first moment Abraham could act on it.
4:
Gill makes the three days do evidential work. Moriah lay some forty miles from Beersheba, so Abraham had travelled two full days, and all that while he had leisure to reconsider what he was about — and by proceeding after so much time to revolve it in his mind he shows he was satisfied that what he had heard was no illusion but an oracle of God, so that his obedience was neither rash nor hasty and his faith was sufficiently tried. Ellicott sets the two weary days beside Hagar's in the wilderness, and marks the difference: hers were human sorrows only, while Abraham was giving up the son on whom his spiritual hopes depended. On seeing the place afar off he answers an objection drawn from the ground itself. The summit usually identified with Moriah cannot be seen from more than three miles away, which has been urged as proof that some more conspicuous hill must be meant; but afar off is used very indefinitely, and three miles agrees exactly with what Abraham did, since he left the servants there, laid the wood on Isaac, and walked the rest — and while three miles would sorely tax a boy carrying wood, from the point where Gerizim first becomes visible it would have been impossible.

That he told the servants he and the lad would come again has always looked like a lie, and the three of them handle it differently. Clarke answers from the epistle, that Abraham accounted God able to raise him up even from the dead, and that it was as easy for God to restore his son after he had been a burnt offering as to have given him life in the beginning — he went therefore fully purposed to offer him, and confidently expecting to have him back. Ellicott says the same and adds that the belief was no novelty to Abraham, the resurrection of the body being part of the creed of both Chaldea and Egypt. Calvin will not smooth it over. The words seem not free from dissimulation; some take them as prophecy, but since Abraham never lost sight of the promise it may be that, trusting in providence, he figured his son to himself as surviving even in death — and since he went as with closed eyes, there is nothing improbable in supposing that he spoke confusedly in a matter so obscure.

Then the boy's question, which Clarke thinks a paraphrase would only spoil, nothing being conceivable more tender than the question of the son and the reply of the father. Calvin calls it a new instrument of torture, and does not doubt that God framed Isaac's tongue to that appellation and directed him to that question, so that nothing might be wanting to the extreme severity of the grief. What he admires is how the knot is untied — by taking refuge in providence — and he turns it into a rule: whenever the Lord gives a command, many things occur to enfeeble our purpose, means fail, we are destitute of counsel, all avenues seem closed, and in such straits the only remedy against despondency is to leave the event to God, that he may open a way where there is none. On the answer itself Ellicott reads the Hebrew as the lamb, and takes Abraham to have meant Isaac, thereby showing that the victim was not of his choosing but God's; Clarke hears prophecy in it, since all other lambs offered from the foundation of the world had been such as men chose and men offered, whereas this was the Lamb which God provided. Wesley turns it into a question to the reader: the fire is ready and the wood is ready, but where is the lamb — where is the heart?
9:
Gill collects the traditions that gathered round the site. Maimonides reports it as a tradition in the hands of all that this is the place where David and Solomon built an altar in the threshing floor of Araunah, where Noah built one on coming out of the ark, where Cain and Abel offered, and where the first man offered when he was created and out of which he was made; the Mahometans, Gill adds, put it at Meena, two or three miles from Mecca, and sacrifice their sheep there on that account. Wesley supplies what the text omits about the altar itself — an altar of earth, we may suppose, the saddest that ever was built.

The binding raises a question the commentators all see. Clarke asks whether Isaac's character has been duly considered, or whether his excellence is lost in the supposition that he was too young to understand his danger and too feeble to resist; he puts his age at about thirty-three, the age at which his great Antitype was offered, and observes that even allowing the twenty-five of Josephus, it cannot be supposed that an old man of a hundred and twenty-five could have bound a young man in the prime of life without his consent. What prevailed here, then, was not the superior strength of the father but the piety and filial obedience of the son. Calvin reaches the same conclusion — Isaac was of middle age and might have been the stronger of the two, so force was not used against a struggling and unwilling youth, but he voluntarily surrendered himself, and can scarcely have done so unless he had already been told what the oracle required. Ellicott reports that the Jewish commentators agree he consented, nor could it well have been otherwise, so that his youthful faith was tried equally with his father's.

Why bind a victim who is willing is Calvin's next question, and he answers it practically: the holy man was anticipating a possible danger, lest something should happen in the middle of the act to interrupt it. Wesley reads the binding typologically instead, that a sacrifice must be bound, and the great Sacrifice to be offered in the fulness of time must be bound, and therefore so must Isaac. What both of them feel is the weight of the scene. Wesley breaks out of exposition into address — be astonished, O heavens, and wonder, O earth, for here is an act of faith and obedience that deserves to be a spectacle to God, angels and men, with Abraham's darling, the church's hope, the heir of promise, lying ready to bleed and die by his own father's hands. Calvin admires the opposite quality in the telling, that the simplicity of the narrative of Moses is wonderful and has greater force than the most exaggerated tragical description; and he puts the sum of the whole in one line, that Abraham, when he had to slay his son, remained always like himself, his fortitude rendering that aged hand equal to a task the very sight of which was enough to destroy his whole body. Gill watches the hand go out, one would think in a trembling manner — for it is enough to make one tremble to think of it.
11:
Henry marks the turn in the weather. Hitherto the story has seemed to hasten toward a tragical end, and here the sky suddenly clears, the sun breaks out, and a bright and pleasant scene opens — the same hand that had wounded and cast down now heals and lifts up. Calvin spots what the scene resembles and refuses the resemblance. The poets, when affairs are desperate in their fables, bring in some god who appears unexpectedly at the critical juncture; and it is possible that Satan, by figments of that kind, has laboured to obscure the wonderful interventions of God, so that the truth has not only been adulterated into a lie but distorted into material for fable, and made the more ridiculous. What actually happened, he says, is that in the very article of death God recalled Isaac from death to life and restored him to his father as one risen from the tomb. On who spoke, most of them agree: Gill takes the Angel for no created angel but the eternal one, the Son of God, and finds it clear from his swearing by himself and renewing the promise in his own name. Ellicott notices something quite different — that the narrative to this point had been Elohistic, and it is the angel of Jehovah who interferes to stop the sacrifice.

Why the hand was stayed at that particular moment Clarke explains by the typology he has been building. Since Isaac was to represent the real sacrifice, it was enough that in his own will and his father's the purpose of the immolation was complete: the father yields up the son, the son gives up his life, and on both sides, so far as will and purpose could go, the sacrifice was finished — God simply spares the father the torture of putting the knife to his son's throat. Gill guards the other flank, that God never meant the boy actually to be slain, since he approves not of human sacrifices, and that the prevention was partly so that the thing might not be drawn into an example, though the Gentiles have imitated it notwithstanding. Henry draws two rules from the timing: our creature-comforts are likeliest to be continued to us when we are most willing to resign them to God's will, and God's time to help his people is when they are brought to the greatest extremity, so that the nearer the danger is to execution, the more welcome the deliverance.

The words now I know that thou fearest God have troubled every reader, and Calvin takes the difficulty head on. Augustine's way out — reading it as I have caused thee to know — he calls forced; but how can anything become known to God, to whom all things have always been present? The answer is condescension: God speaks of what he has proved by experiment as now made known to himself, not according to his own infinite wisdom but according to our infirmity, and what Moses means is simply that Abraham by this act testified how reverently he feared God. Nor were the earlier proofs insufficient in themselves; it is rather that when God willed him to proceed this far, the trial was at last complete, where in other persons a much lighter one would have sufficed. Henry says the same more briefly, that God knew it before but Abraham has now given a most memorable evidence of it and need do no more — and adds the consolation that when God by his providence hinders the performance of our sincere intentions in his service, he graciously accepts the will for the deed. Calvin's own lesson is about the ceasing: it was not lawful for Abraham either to undertake or to relinquish anything except by God's authority, so let God prescribe to us our manner both of acting and of ceasing to act.
13:
Ellicott begins with the text. By a slight change in the shape of one consonant many ancient authorities read one ram rather than a ram behind, a correction he calls almost certain, since nowhere else is the word rendered behind used as an adverb of place; and the animal was probably the four-horned kind still common in the East. What he finds in the substitution is the doctrine itself — the ram took Isaac's place and by its actual death completed the typical representation, and there is no difficulty in the type being composed of two parts, what was wanting in Isaac supplied by the ram. Had Isaac actually died by his father's hand it would have been unbearable, and the possibility of a vicarious sacrifice taught less clearly rather than more; so he rises again to life from the altar while the ram dies in his stead, and the two together set forth the whole mystery. Calvin dismisses the rabbinic story that the ram had been created on the sixth day of the world as of a piece with the rest of their fictions, but does not doubt it was presented there by miracle; and he keeps his own moral modest — since a ram is substituted, God shows us as in a glass the design of our mortification, that by the Spirit dwelling in us we, though dead, may yet be living sacrifices. More subtle allegories can be elicited, he adds, but he does not see what they rest on.

The name Abraham gave the place turns on whether the verb is active or passive. Clarke gives it literally as the Lord will see, whence the usual rendering that the Lord will provide, since his eye ever affects his heart and the wants he sees his hand is ready to supply; but he thinks the words were spoken prophetically, and prefers with Houbigant the Lord shall be seen, which the clause that follows seems to require — on this mount the Lord shall be seen. Ellicott sets the versions side by side: the Samaritan, Syriac and Vulgate read in the mount Jehovah will provide, which changes none of the consonants but only the vowels, added since the Christian era; while the Greek, without touching the vowels at all, has in the mount Jehovah shall be seen, which would make it a prophecy of the manifestation of Christ. Gill notices the tense, the future standing for the past, so that the name records what God has just done and promises what he will do.

Calvin refuses to choose and holds both senses together. The change of the name in process of time was deliberate and no mistake, and those who turned the active into a passive meant to teach that God not only looks upon his own but makes his help manifest to them, so that in turn he may be seen by them: the seeing has precedence, since by his secret providence he determines what is best for us, but the being seen hangs upon it, since he stretches out his hand and renders himself visible by experimental tokens. Wesley says it in the shorter form — the Lord will see, and will be seen in the mount, in the greatest perplexities of his people; where God sees and provides, he should be seen and praised. Ellicott asks the question none of the others do: when and how did the saying grow into a proverb, and who added the note? Possibly Moses, when he arranged these documents; less probably Ezra and the men of the Great Synagogue. Either way the proverb is a national testimony to the genuineness of the record, proving that the facts were so impressed on the memory of Abraham's descendants as to shape their thoughts and their language.
15:
The oath is the striking thing, and the commentators say why. Keil notes that Jehovah's swearing by himself never occurs again in his dealings with the patriarchs, and that later scripture keeps referring back to it — Luther held that everything said in the psalms about the oath given to David rests on this one, since in the promise those psalms are built on no oath is mentioned at all. Ellicott makes the same point as an argument: this is the sole instance of such an interposition in Holy Scripture, which plainly indicates that the trial was of no common kind and its typical teaching of no ordinary value. Henry marks the escalation — the thing was said and sealed before, and now it is sworn; God interposed himself by an oath and, to speak with reverence, even pawned his own life and being upon it, that by all those immutable things his people might have strong consolation. If we exercise faith, he adds, God will encourage it; improve the promises, and God will ratify them.

Calvin sees a difficulty the others pass over. What had been promised freely before Isaac was born is here spoken of as a reward — because thou hast done this thing — and grace and reward are incompatible; since the blessing promised in the seed contains the hope of salvation, it might seem to follow that eternal life is given in return for good works, and the Papists, he says, boldly seize on the passage. His answer is to turn the argument round. If the promise was gratuitous before and is now ascribed to a reward, then whatever God grants to good works should be received as from grace; and if Abraham earned so great a compensation by his own virtue, the grace which anticipated him is made of none effect. What is freely given is yet called the reward of works — not to obscure the glory of God's goodness but to excite his people to the love of well-doing, when they perceive their acts of duty so far pleasing to him as to obtain a reward, while he pays nothing as a debt and merely gives his own benefits that title. The Lord shows himself doubly liberal, transferring to our works what properly belongs to his own pure beneficence. Henry states the same balance in a sentence: this was no proportionable consideration, but God graciously put that honour upon what had honoured him.

On the promises themselves Henry counts four — the blessing of the Spirit, the increase of the church, spiritual victories, and the incarnation, since in thy seed means one particular person and not many, as the apostle observes. Possessing the gate of the enemies Clarke reads broadly, the gates standing for all their strength, whether troops or counsels or fortified cities, and he suspects our Lord had this very promise in view when he said the gates of hell should not prevail. Calvin agrees on the sense — the gates were their bulwarks and the place where judgment was administered — and adds the qualification he thinks indispensable, that the victory is promised not to Abraham's sons promiscuously but to Christ and his members so far as they adhere under one Head, since without some mark distinguishing the legitimate from the degenerate sons the promise would take in Ishmaelites and Idumeans equally with Israel. Ellicott sums up what is new here in three points: the blessing is no longer a promise but a compact ratified by oath, it assures the seed of victory, and it transfers to Abraham's offspring the office of being the means of blessedness to all mankind.
19:
Gill notices an absence. Isaac is not mentioned in the return, though there is no doubt he came back with his father, since we hear of him in the house afterwards; and the Targum of Jonathan's account — that the angels took him and brought him to the school of Shem the great, where he stayed three years — cannot be depended on. Calvin reads the quiet at Beersheba as part of the story rather than a coda: this notice is inserted, along with what follows about the increase of Abraham's kindred, to show that the holy man, brought up again from the abyss of death, was made happy in more ways than one, God so reviving him that he should be like a new man.

Why a family list should follow so great a scene is answered the same way by nearly all of them. Clarke says it is introduced solely to prepare the reader for what comes next, and to show that providence was preparing, in one of the branches of Abraham's family, a suitable spouse for his son; Calvin puts it that Moses records the progeny of Nahor because Isaac was to take his wife from it, adding that the mention of women in scripture is rare, and it is credible that many daughters were born to Nahor of whom one only is introduced here. Ellicott adds the human circumstance — dwelling so far apart, news would seldom reach Abraham, and besides the domestic interest the knowledge was probably what decided him to seek a wife for his son among his own kindred. Henry finds something else in it worth having: though Abraham saw his own family dignified with peculiar privileges, admitted into covenant and blessed with the entail of the promise, he did not look upon his relations with contempt or disdain, but was glad to hear of the increase and prosperity of their households.

The names themselves divide the commentators. Gill takes Huz for the founder of the land of Uz where Job dwelt and Buz for the father of the Buzites, Elihu's family, and reports the common view that the Chaldees sprang from Chesed — while noting the difficulty, that the Chaldees are mentioned before this man was born, unless they are so named by anticipation. Clarke adds the Greek reading that makes Kemuel father of the Syrians. Ellicott denies both identifications: Kemuel was not the progenitor of the Aramaic race but the ancestor of the family of Ram to which Elihu belonged, and Chesed was not the ancestor of the ancient Chaldees but possibly of the small tribe of robbers of the same name who plundered Job — of the rest, he says flatly, no trace remains in history. He also notices a pattern and refuses to build on it: Nahor has twelve sons, eight by his wife and four by his concubine, as Jacob has twelve by two wives and two concubines, and Ishmael twelve; the coincidences are curious but afford no ground for calling the narratives mythical, since coincidences quite as strange are found in every history and in daily life. Calvin explains the concubine's sons being listed apart as occupying a less honourable place, and refuses to let the custom justify itself: that it entered Nahor's mind to take a second wife does not make polygamy lawful, but only shows he supposed lawful for himself what had really sprung from the worst corruption.
